1051.title: Michaelmas (29 September)
1051.hook: the feast of Michael and all angels
1051.howItsDone: Churches that keep Michaelmas read the scriptures of Michael and of angels, and some pray traditional prayers to Saint Michael or about guardian angels; in some places the day also keeps old customs of the autumn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Cross Day, and a cross honored as a tree. Your line was the tree of life. Which tree did you stop beside? Day one thousand fifty-one.

Some universities still call their autumn term the Michaelmas term. Tradition says older calendars treated the day as a turning point of the year, when accounts were settled. And there's a folk saying, told with a straight face in parts of Britain, that you shouldn't pick blackberries after Michaelmas, because by then they've been spoiled. A feast that ended up in term names and berry picking. Its full name in some prayer books is longer and stranger: the feast of Saint Michael and all angels. Today, Michaelmas.
screen: `A TERM, A SETTLING DAY, A BLACKBERRY RULE.`

segments.voice: Michael is one of the angels the Bible calls by name. In Daniel he is "the great prince" who stands up for his people. The letter of Jude calls him "Michael the archangel." And in Revelation, in a vision, "there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon." So Michael is the angel of standing up, of holding the line. But the feast doesn't stop with Michael. It's for all angels, and plenty of the Bible's angels arrive without swords. In story after story they come as messengers. They turn up with news, with food, with a hand on the shoulder. Which brings us to the carry, from the letter to the Hebrews: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares. Without knowing. Some readers hear in that verse an old story from Genesis. Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. He looks up and sees three men standing near. The text doesn't say he knows who they are. It says "he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground." He brings water for their feet, bread, a calf, milk. As the story goes on, the text has the LORD speaking to Abraham. So the feast holds two pictures. Michael, standing against the dark. And strangers at a tent door, who might be more than they seem. Christians differ in how much they say about angels. Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks readily of guardian angels; some Protestants say less, and keep close to texts like the psalm: "he shall give his angels charge over thee." On this day, some simply give thanks for help they never saw coming.

Here's the practice: give thanks for unseen help. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last week or so, and find one moment when help arrived that you didn't arrange. Someone held a door, or texted at the right time, or a stranger pointed the way. Maybe you never learned their name. Stay with that moment. Let yourself see their face, if you can. If you pray, you can thank God for that help and for the person who brought it. If you don't, just hold them in mind with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Michaelmas. The feast of Saint Michael and all angels, for the archangel who stands up, and for the messengers who arrive as strangers.
Your line: angels unawares. Today, treat one stranger the way Abraham did: notice them, make a little room, offer something, even just your attention. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: Blessing of the animals (4 October)
1052.hook: on Francis's day, churches bless pets and farm animals
1052.howItsDone: On or near the feast of Francis of Assisi, some Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches hold a blessing of the animals, where people bring pets or farm animals and a priest or minister blesses each one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Michaelmas, Michael and all angels, and strangers at a tent door. Your line was angels unawares. Which stranger did you make a little room for? Day one thousand fifty-two.

A church parking lot on a Sunday afternoon. A line of people waits in the sun. A spaniel on a red leash. A boy with a goldfish in a jam jar. An elderly woman with a cat that clearly did not agree to come. Someone has brought a chicken under one arm. A tortoise is being carried in a shoebox. At the front, a minister or priest bends down to each one, says a few words, and sometimes sprinkles a little water. The cat objects. The spaniel tries to lick the prayer book. It happens on or near the feast of Francis of Assisi, who called the creatures his brothers and sisters. Today, the Blessing of the animals.

Why bless a goldfish? The answer starts on the Bible's first page. On the sixth day in Genesis, God says, in the King James Bible, "Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind." And the refrain comes again: God saw that it was good. Animals aren't scenery in the story. They are made and called good before any human is there to use them. Now a detail hidden in the Hebrew. The words for living creature are nefesh chayah. In the next chapter, when God breathes into the first human, the King James says "man became a living soul," and the Hebrew there uses the same phrase, nefesh chayah. English splits it into creature and soul. Hebrew gives humans and animals the same two words. The Bible keeps the animals in God's care after that. After the flood, God's promise is made with Noah "and with every living creature that is with you." A psalm says, "O LORD, thou preservest man and beast." And Jesus says a sparrow, sold cheap, "shall not fall on the ground without your Father." Then Francis. His early biographers tell of him calling animals brother and sister, and there's a story in the Little Flowers about a wolf that troubled the town of Gubbio, whom Francis called brother wolf and made peace with. Whatever you make of the wolf, the habit is the point. Not it. Not livestock. Brother. So a blessing of the animals isn't a joke service, even when the cat is yowling. It says out loud what Genesis said first: this living creature is God's, and it is good. In Francis's spirit, the spaniel on the red leash becomes brother dog.

Here's the practice: bless an animal, or hold one in mind. Settle, and breathe. If there's an animal near you right now, a dog at your feet, a cat on the sofa, a bird outside the window, look at it for a while. Notice how it breathes. If there isn't one, bring to mind an animal you've known and loved. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that creature, or ask God's blessing on it in your own words. If you don't, just watch, or remember, with care and thanks. The bell holds the time.
Nefesh chayah. Hebrew for a living creature, the same two words the Bible uses for the first human, and for every animal blessed on this day.
Your line: brother dog. Today, call one animal you meet brother or sister, out loud or under your breath, and treat it that way. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: Teresa's day (15 October)
1053.hook: her bookmark: let nothing disturb you, God alone suffices
1053.howItsDone: Catholics keep Teresa of Ávila's feast in October with readings from her writings, and some Anglicans and Lutherans remember her too; her bookmark lines are often printed on cards and prayed or sung, as in a Taizé chant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nefesh chayah, and a Hebrew phrase shared by people and creatures. Your line was brother dog. Which animal did you greet that way? Day one thousand fifty-three.

A slip of paper, small enough to mark a page, with a few lines on it in Spanish. Tradition says it was found tucked in the prayer book of a nun from Ávila after she died, and that she had kept it there to read. The lines say: don't be disturbed, don't be afraid, everything passes. And at the bottom, three words that people still copy onto cards and walls. The nun was Teresa of Ávila, and the Catholic Church keeps her feast in October. Today, Teresa's day, and the words on her bookmark.
screen: `A SLIP OF PAPER IN A PRAYER BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in a plain paraphrase. Let nothing disturb you. Let nothing frighten you. All things are passing. God does not change. Patience gains everything. Whoever has God lacks nothing. God alone is enough. In Spanish, that last line is three words: solo Dios basta. Basta is the word you'd shout to stop an argument: enough! Teresa turns it around. Not enough of this. Enough, because of God. Notice what the bookmark doesn't say. It doesn't say nothing bad will happen. It says things will pass. It doesn't say don't feel. It says don't let it take you over. Tradition remembers her life as busy and bumpy, with hard travel, illness and opposition, not a quiet garden. The bookmark reads like something kept close because it was needed daily. The Bible has the same note in more than one place. A psalm: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." I shall not want: I won't lack anything. And Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, says that when he begged to be rid of some weakness, the answer came: "My grace is sufficient for thee." Sufficient. Enough. The same thought in another key. Catholics honor Teresa as a saint and as a teacher of prayer, and some Anglicans and Lutherans remember her too. But the bookmark itself is for anyone who has ever stood in a kitchen at two in the morning, heart racing over a bill or a test result. It doesn't argue. In Teresa's voice, it just says: this will pass. God doesn't. God alone suffices.
screen: `SOLO DIOS BASTA: GOD ALONE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a bookmark. Find a scrap of paper, a receipt, a sticky note, anything. Settle, and breathe. Write one line from Teresa's bookmark, whichever one you need today. Let nothing disturb you. All things are passing. God alone suffices. If you don't share her faith, you might write all things are passing. Then put the pen down and read it slowly, three or four times, letting each word land. If you pray, you can hold your worries up against it, one at a time. If you don't, simply let the line sit beside them. Then tuck it in a book you're reading. The bell holds the time.
Teresa's day. The feast of Teresa of Ávila, remembered for the bookmark found in her prayer book, which ends: God alone suffices.
Your line: god alone suffices. Today, when something starts to disturb you, open the book and find the bookmark. Read it once, slowly. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: Reformation Day (31 October)
1054.hook: Lutherans and others remember 1517, now often with Catholic neighbors
1054.howItsDone: Lutheran and some other Protestant churches keep Reformation Day at the end of October with hymns and readings on grace and faith, and in some places Lutherans and Catholics now hold joint services of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's day, and a slip of paper in a prayer book. Your line was god alone suffices. Did you reach for the bookmark? Day one thousand fifty-four.

What does it take for a church to say, out loud, we need fixing? On the last day of October, while some streets fill with costumes and pumpkins, Lutheran churches and others keep a quieter anniversary. Tradition says that on the eve of All Saints, a friar and teacher named Martin Luther posted a set of theses, points for debate, on the church door in Wittenberg, in Germany, questioning the sale of indulgences, which Catholic teaching describes as release from punishment still due for sins already forgiven. What followed split Western Christianity. And in recent years, in some places, Lutherans and Catholics have begun marking the day side by side. Today, Reformation Day.

For Luther, much turned on a verse. In Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James Bible: "The just shall live by faith." Luther came to read it as good news: that God makes people right as a gift, received by trust, not bought or earned. Ephesians puts it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." So when he saw indulgences being sold, he objected. The argument grew far beyond what one set of theses could hold. Churches divided. The years that followed were bitter, and in places bloody, on more than one side. That history is part of the day, and it's honest to say so. Then the carry. Semper reformanda, a Latin motto later taken up in Reformed churches. In full it's often given as: the church reformed, and always being reformed. The point is that reform is not a single event in the past. On this view, a church that thinks it has finished reforming has stopped listening. Paul's line in Romans fits it: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Some readers hear that as ongoing, not once. Catholics have their own way of saying this. The Second Vatican Council spoke of Christ calling the church to continual reformation, as it goes on its pilgrim way. Lutherans and Catholics have since signed a joint statement on how God makes sinners right, and some now pray together on this day, with thanks for what each has received, and sorrow for the wounds of division. Different churches, still different in real ways. But on one point they can say the same words: always being reformed.

Here's the practice: pray for your own church's reform. Not someone else's. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a community you belong to: a church, if you have one, or a family, a team, a workplace. Name one thing in it that needs mending. Keep it specific, and keep it close to home. Then name one part you play in it, however small. If you pray, you can ask God to reform your church, beginning with you. If you don't, just hold that one thing, and your part in it, honestly, without blame. The bell holds the time.
Reformation Day. The day Lutherans and others remember Martin Luther's theses and the reform that followed, kept now, in some places, alongside Catholic neighbors.
Your line: semper reformanda. Always being reformed. Today, fix one small thing in a place you belong, without waiting for anyone else to go first. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: All Saints (1 November)
1055.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches keep a feast of all the saints, often singing 'For All the Saints'; Orthodox churches keep their All Saints Sunday after Pentecost rather than in November.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reformation Day, and a church that keeps saying it needs mending. Your line was semper reformanda. What small thing did you fix? Day one thousand fifty-five.

Paul opens a letter to a small church in a Roman town with a greeting that sounds too grand for it: "To all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi." Not just to the leaders. Not to a few heroes. To all the saints. He means the people in the room: a businesswoman who traded in purple, a jailer and his household, some who were quarreling with each other. Ordinary people, meeting in a house, called saints. Later the church would keep feast days for famous names, one after another, through the year. And then one day for the rest. Every saint, known and unknown. Today, All Saints.

In the New Testament, saint means holy one, someone set apart for God, and Paul uses it for whole congregations. Over time, the church also came to use the word for particular people whose lives shone, and to give some of them a day. But a calendar has only so many days, and plenty of faithful people left no name anyone remembers. All Saints is the feast for all of them at once. The letter to the Hebrews gives the picture. After a long list of faithful people from Israel's story, it says: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." Like runners in a stadium, with the stands packed with those who have already finished the race. Revelation widens it further. John sees "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues," standing before the throne. No one could count them. That's the crowd this day honors. Churches keep it differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor the saints and ask them to pray for them, as you might ask a friend. Protestant churches tend to remember the saints as examples and companions, giving thanks for them, without asking for their prayers. And in some of these churches, a hymn is sung on this day that begins, for all the saints. Here, at least, the churches can meet. On this day, the saints aren't only the famous ones in stained glass. The day remembers the grandmother who prayed every night, the teacher who stayed late, the neighbor who quietly kept faith. Paul's greeting at Philippi went to people just like them.

Here's the practice: name the saints in your own life. Settle, and breathe. Let the faces come: people who showed you, by how they lived, what goodness or faith looks like. Maybe a grandparent. A teacher. A friend who stayed. Someone you met once and never forgot. Say their names, quietly, one at a time, and leave a little space after each. Some are living; some have died. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for each of them. If you don't, simply give thanks for them, and let the stands fill up. The bell holds the time.
All Saints. The feast for every saint, known and unknown: the whole cloud of witnesses, a multitude no one could number.
Your line: for all the saints. Today, tell one of the people you named that they matter to you. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: All Souls (2 November)
1056.hook: many churches remember all the faithful departed, and families visit graves
1056.howItsDone: On All Souls, Catholics and some Anglicans pray for the faithful departed and offer Masses or services for them; in some countries families clean and decorate graves and light candles, and some churches read out the names of those who died in the past year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Saints, every saint, known and unknown. Your line was for all the saints. Whose name did you say out loud? Day one thousand fifty-six.

Dusk in a cemetery. A woman kneels and pulls weeds from around a stone, then wipes the name with her sleeve. Her son sets a candle in a red glass jar at the foot of the grave and shields the match from the wind. Across the rows, other little flames come on, one by one, until the whole hillside flickers. Someone has brought flowers. Someone has brought a thermos. Nobody is in a hurry. In some countries, this is what the second day of November looks like. Yesterday the church remembered the saints. Today it remembers everyone else who has died in faith. Today, All Souls.
screen: `A CANDLE IN A RED GLASS JAR.`

segments.voice: All Saints and All Souls sit side by side on purpose. One day for the cloud of witnesses. The next for the faithful departed: grandparents, friends, a child, the people whose graves we know. Grief comes first. At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, in John's Gospel, the King James Bible says it in two words: "Jesus wept." He knows what he's about to do, and he weeps anyway. In the story, grief isn't a lack of faith. And earlier in the same chapter, the hope: "I am the resurrection, and the life." Paul holds both together when he writes to the church in Thessalonica about those who have died. He doesn't tell them not to grieve. He tells them "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." Sorrow, yes. But sorrow with hope in it. Churches keep this day in different ways. Catholics pray for the dead, trusting that God's mercy can still be at work in them, purifying them, and on this day Masses are offered for all the faithful departed. Orthodox Christians pray for the departed too, in memorial services held through the year. Protestant churches differ. Some don't pray for the dead and instead give thanks for their lives and entrust them to God; some, including some Anglicans, keep All Souls with prayers. In some places, families go to the graves, clean them, and light candles. The carry comes from an old prayer of the Western church, which asks God to give the dead eternal rest, and to let perpetual light shine on them. In Latin it begins with the word requiem, rest. That's why a Mass for the dead is called a requiem. Rest, and light. Two gifts asked for those we can't hold anymore.

Here's the practice: light a candle for someone who has died. If you can, light a real one now, safely, or switch on a small lamp. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has died. Say their name. Let one ordinary memory come: their laugh, their hands, a phrase they always used. Let whatever you feel be there. If you pray, you can use the old words: rest eternal grant unto them, and let light shine on them. If you don't, simply watch the flame, and hold them in it. The bell holds the time.
All Souls. The day after All Saints, when churches remember all the faithful departed, and families visit graves and light candles.
Your line: rest eternal. Today, say the name of someone who has died to someone who knew them, or visit a grave, or leave the candle burning a little longer. Day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: Remembrance
1057.hook: poppies, silence, and prayers for all who died in war
1057.howItsDone: In some countries, churches hold Remembrance services with poppies, a two-minute silence at a memorial, names of the dead read aloud, and prayers for peace and for all who died in war.

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Souls: candles lit and graves visited for the faithful departed. Your line was rest eternal. Whose name did you hold in the light? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

A red paper flower, pinned to a coat. Then another, on a bus driver. Another on a newsreader. In some countries, poppies like these bloom on coats each autumn, and then, on one morning, a whole street goes quiet. Traffic stops. A shop falls silent mid-sale. At a stone memorial, someone reads a poem, and the crowd answers it with a few plain words: we will remember them. Churches keep this day too. Prayers are said for all who died in war, soldiers and civilians, names known and names lost. It's a morning when the church brings its own words to a nation's silence. Today's word: Remembrance.

Start with the flower. An old war poem, In Flanders Fields, sees poppies blowing between rows of crosses over the graves of the dead. The red poppy people wear grew, so the usual account goes, out of that picture. It isn't a Bible symbol. But the church found it already had words for this day. First, silence. Ecclesiastes has a whole poem of times and seasons, and in the middle of it, in the King James words: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." At Remembrance, the silence comes first, before any speech or name. Second, love. On the night before he died, Jesus told his friends: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Some memorials carry that line, cut into stone. Many Christians hear it first about Jesus himself, and then about anyone who gave their life for someone else. Third, hope. Remembrance is not a celebration of war. The prophet Isaiah saw a day when the nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Some churches read that line at Remembrance, and pray for the dead of every side. Christians disagree about war. Some churches accept that a nation may fight to defend the weak; others refuse to bear arms at all, and keep this day with their whole weight on peace. Both can stand in the same silence. And for many Christians, that silence isn't empty. It's a kind of prayer: holding the dead before God, and asking for fewer names to read next time.

Here's the practice: keep two minutes' silence. The bell will hold just that. Stand if you can, or sit very still. Bring to mind one person who died in a war: a face in an old family photo, a name on a memorial you pass, someone from the news. If no name comes, hold the ones nobody remembers. Don't fill the silence with thinking. Let it be heavy. If you pray, you can hold them before God, with Isaiah's hope: neither shall they learn war any more. If you don't, just stand with them. The bell holds the time.
Remembrance. Standing still together for all who died in war, with poppies, silence, and prayer for peace.
Your line: we will remember. Today, find one name on a war memorial, a plaque, or in your family's story, and read it slowly, once, all the way through. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

in John's Gospel, Jesus says it to his friends, on the night before he died.

fork.setup: in Isaiah's vision, the nations come with swords and spears. what do they do with them?
options: hang them up in the temple as trophies.
beat them into plowshares and pruninghooks.
bury them where no one will find them.
fork.reveal: they beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruninghooks: farm tools, for feeding people. and they learn war no more.

original.note: Hebrew: to remember. in the Bible, remembering can be something you do, not only something you think.

trapdoor: what you thought: a day for the past, poppies and old soldiers.
what it means: standing still together for all who died in war, and asking for peace, so there are fewer names to read.
what a scholar hears: the church brings old words to a civic day: a time to keep silence, greater love hath no man, swords into plowshares.
